L40: 
L41: Return `True` if all elements of the iterable are true (or if the iterable is empty). Equivalent to:
L42: 
L43:     def all(iterable):
L44:         for element in iterable:

L72: bin(integer, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【7†¶】
L73: Convert an integer number to a binary string prefixed with “0b”. The result is a valid Python expression. If integer is not a Python 【37†`int`】 object, it has to define an 【81†`__index__()`】 method that returns an integer. Some examples:

L77:     >>> bin(-10)

L82:     ('0b1110', '1110')

If the argument is false or omitted, this returns `False`; otherwise, it returns `True`. The `bool` class is a subclass of 【37†`int`】 (see 【84†Numeric Types — int, float, complex】). L95: breakpoint(*args, **kws)【9†¶】
L96: This function drops you into the debugger at the call site. Specifically, it calls 【86†`sys.breakpointhook()`】, passing `args` and `kws` straight through. By default, `sys.breakpointhook()` calls 【87†`pdb.set_trace()`】 expecting no arguments. In this case, it is purely a convenience function so you don’t have to explicitly import 【88†`pdb`】 or type as much code to enter the debugger.
L97: However, `sys.breakpointhook()` can be set to some other function and `breakpoint()` will automatically call that, allowing you to drop into the debugger of choice. If `sys.breakpointhook()` is not accessible, this function will raise 【89†`RuntimeError`】.
L98: By default, the behavior of `breakpoint()` can be changed with the 【90†`PYTHONBREAKPOINT`】 environment variable. See 【86†`sys.breakpointhook()`】 for usage details.
L99: 
L100: Note that this is not guaranteed if 【86†`sys.breakpointhook()`】 has been replaced.
L101: 
L102: Raises an 【91†auditing event】 `builtins.breakpoint` with argument `breakpointhook`.

L107: class bytearray(source, encoding, errors='strict')
L108: Return a new array of bytes. The 【92†`bytearray`】 class is a mutable sequence of integers in the range 0 <= x < 256. It has most of the usual methods of mutable sequences, described in 【93†Mutable Sequence Types】, as well as most methods that the 【94†`bytes`】 type has, see 【95†Bytes and Bytearray Operations】.
L109: 
L110: The optional source parameter can be used to initialize the array in a few different ways:
L111:   * If it is a string, you must also give the encoding (and optionally, errors) parameters; 【92†`bytearray()`】 then converts the string to bytes using 【96†`str.encode()`】.
L112: 
L113:   * If it is an integer, the array will have that size and will be initialized with null bytes.
L114: 
L115:   * If it is an object conforming to the 【97†buffer interface】, a read-only buffer of the object will be used to initialize the bytes array.
L116:   * If it is an iterable, it must be an iterable of integers in the range `0 <= x < 256`, which are used as the initial contents of the array.
L117: 
L118: Without an argument, an array of size 0 is created.

L120: See also 【98†Binary Sequence Types — bytes, bytearray, memoryview】 and 【99†Bytearray Objects】.

L125: 
L126: Accordingly, constructor arguments are interpreted as for 【92†`bytearray()`】.

If this returns `True`, it is still possible that a call fails, but if it is `False`, calling object will never succeed. Note that classes are callable (calling a class returns a new instance); instances are callable if their class has a 【104†`__call__()`】 method.

L142: @classmethod【14†¶】
L143: 
L144: 
L145: Transform a method into a class method.
L146: A class method receives the class as an implicit first argument, just like an instance method receives the instance. To declare a class method, use this idiom:
L147: 
L148:     class C:
L149:         @classmethod
L150:         def f(cls, arg1, arg2): ...
L151: 
L152: 
L153: The `@classmethod` form is a function 【106†decorator】 – see 【107†Function definitions】 for details.
L154: A class method can be called either on the class (such as `C.f()`) or on an instance (such as `C().f()`). The instance is ignored except for its class. If a class method is called for a derived class, the derived class object is passed as the implied first argument.
L155: 
L156: Class methods are different than C++ or Java static methods. If you want those, see 【65†`staticmethod()`】 in this section. For more information on class methods, see 【108†The standard type hierarchy】.
L157: Changed in version 3.9: Class methods can now wrap other 【109†descriptors】 such as 【55†`property()`】.
L158: 
L159: Changed in version 3.10: Class methods now inherit the method attributes (【110†`__module__`】, 【111†`__name__`】, 【112†`__qualname__`】, 【113†`__doc__`】 and 【114†`__annotations__`】) and have a new `__wrapped__` attribute.
L160: 
L161: Deprecated since version 3.11, removed in version 3.13: Class methods can no longer wrap other 【109†descriptors】 such as 【55†`property()`】.
L162: compile(source, filename, mode, flags=0, dont_inherit=False, optimize=-1, * (Keyword-only parameters separator (PEP 3102)), module=None)【15†¶】
L163: 
L164: 
L165: Compile the source into a code or AST object. Code objects can be executed by 【23†`exec()`】 or 【22†`eval()`】. source can either be a normal string, a byte string, or an AST object. Refer to the 【115†`ast`】 module documentation for information on how to work with AST objects.
L166: The filename argument should give the file from which the code was read; pass some recognizable value if it wasn’t read from a file (`'<string>'` is commonly used).
L167: The mode argument specifies what kind of code must be compiled; it can be `'exec'` if source consists of a sequence of statements, `'eval'` if it consists of a single expression, or `'single'` if it consists of a single interactive statement (in the latter case, expression statements that evaluate to something other than `None` will be printed). It can also be `'func_type'` if source consists of a function type signature, for example `(int) -> str`; see 【116†`ast.parse()`】 for more information.
L168: This mode requires passing 【117†`ast.PyCF_ONLY_AST`】 in flags.
L169: The optional arguments flags and dont_inherit control which 【118†compiler options】 should be activated and which 【119†future features】 should be allowed. If neither is present (or both are zero) the code is compiled with the same flags that affect the code that is calling `compile()`. If the flags argument is given and dont_inherit is not (or is zero) then the compiler options and the future statements specified by the flags argument are used in addition to those that would be used anyway.
L170: If dont_inherit is a non-zero integer then the flags argument is it – the flags (future features and compiler options) in the surrounding code are ignored.
L171: Compiler options and future statements are specified by bits which can be bitwise ORed together to specify multiple options. The bitfield required to specify a given future feature can be found as the 【120†`compiler_flag`】 attribute on the 【121†`_Feature`】 instance in the 【122†`__future__`】 module. 【118†Compiler flags】 can be found in 【115†`ast`】 module, with `PyCF_` prefix.
L172: The argument optimize specifies the optimization level of the compiler; the default value of `-1` selects the optimization level of the interpreter as given by 【123†`-O`】 options. Explicit levels are `0` (no optimization; `__debug__` is true), `1` (asserts are removed, `__debug__` is false) or `2` (docstrings are removed too).
L173: 
L174: The optional argument module specifies the module name. It is needed to unambiguous 【124†filter】 syntax warnings by module name.
L175: This function raises 【125†`SyntaxError`】 if the compiled source is invalid, including a source containing a null character or that cannot be decoded; 【105†`ValueError`】 if mode or flags is invalid, or if a string source contains surrogate characters; 【126†`MemoryError`】 or 【127†`RecursionError`】 if source is too complex to parse or compile, for example an expression with many thousands of nested operators; and 【128†`OverflowError`】 if source is too large.
L176: If you want to parse Python code into its AST representation, see 【116†`ast.parse()`】.
L177: 
L178: Raises an 【91†auditing event】 `compile` with arguments `source` and `filename`. This event may also be raised by implicit compilation.
L179: 
L180: Note
L181: 
L182: When compiling a string with multi-line code in `'single'` or `'eval'` mode, input must be terminated by at least one newline character. This is to facilitate detection of incomplete and complete statements in the 【129†`code`】 module.
L183: 
L184: Warning
L185: It is possible to crash the Python interpreter with a sufficiently large/complex string when compiling to an AST object due to stack depth limitations in Python’s AST compiler.
L186: 
L187: Changed in version 3.2: Allowed use of Windows and Mac newlines. Also, input in `'exec'` mode does not have to end in a newline anymore. Added the optimize parameter.
L188: 
L189: Changed in version 3.5: Previously, 【130†`TypeError`】 was raised when null bytes were encountered in source.
L190: Changed in version 3.8: `ast.PyCF_ALLOW_TOP_LEVEL_AWAIT` can now be passed in flags to enable support for top-level `await`, `async for`, and `async with`.
L191: 
L192: Changed in version 3.8: Added support for `mode='func_type'`.
L193: 
L194: Changed in version 3.12: 【125†`SyntaxError`】 is raised instead of 【105†`ValueError`】 when null bytes are encountered in source.
L195: 
L196: Changed in version 3.15: Added the module parameter.
L197: class complex(number=0, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【16†¶】
L198: class complex(string, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))
L199: class complex(real=0, imag=0)
L200: 
L201: 
L202: Convert a single string or number to a complex number, or create a complex number from real and imaginary parts.
L203: Examples:
L204: 
L205:     >>> complex('+1.23')
L206:     (1.23+0j)
L207:     >>> complex('-4.5j')
L208:     -4.5j
L209:     >>> complex('-1.23+4.5j')
L210:     (-1.23+4.5j)
L211:     >>> complex('\t( -1.23+4.5J )\n')
L212:     (-1.23+4.5j)
L213:     >>> complex('-Infinity+NaNj')
L214:     (-inf+nanj)
L215:     >>> complex(1.23)
L216:     (1.23+0j)
L217:     >>> complex(imag=-4.5)
L218:     -4.5j
L219:     >>> complex(-1.23, 4.5)
L220:     (-1.23+4.5j)
L221: If the argument is a string, it must contain either a real part (in the same format as for 【25†`float()`】) or an imaginary part (in the same format but with a `'j'` or `'J'` suffix), or both real and imaginary parts (the sign of the imaginary part is mandatory in this case). The string can optionally be surrounded by whitespaces and the round parentheses `'('` and `')'`, which are ignored. The string must not contain whitespace between `'+'`, `'-'`, the `'j'` or `'J'` suffix, and the decimal number.
L222: For example, `complex('1+2j')` is fine, but `complex('1 + 2j')` raises 【105†`ValueError`】. More precisely, the input must conform to the 【131†`complexvalue`】 production rule in the following grammar, after parentheses and leading and trailing whitespace characters are removed:
L223: 
L224:     complexvalue: 【132†`floatvalue`】 |
L225:                   【132†`floatvalue`】 ("j" | "J") |
L226:                   【132†`floatvalue`】 【133†`sign`】 【134†`absfloatvalue`】 ("j" | "J")
L227: If the argument is a number, the constructor serves as a numeric conversion like 【37†`int`】 and 【25†`float`】. For a general Python object `x`, `complex(x)` delegates to `x.__complex__()`. If 【135†`__complex__()`】 is not defined then it falls back to 【136†`__float__()`】. If `__float__()` is not defined then it falls back to 【81†`__index__()`】.
L228: If two arguments are provided or keyword arguments are used, each argument may be any numeric type (including complex). If both arguments are real numbers, return a complex number with the real component real and the imaginary component imag. If both arguments are complex numbers, return a complex number with the real component `real.real-imag.imag` and the imaginary component `real.imag+imag.real`. If one of arguments is a real number, only its real component is used in the above expressions.
L229: See also 【137†`complex.from_number()`】 which only accepts a single numeric argument.
L230: 
L231: If all arguments are omitted, returns `0j`.
L232: 
L233: The complex type is described in 【84†Numeric Types — int, float, complex】.
L234: 
L235: Changed in version 3.6: Grouping digits with underscores as in code literals is allowed.
L236: 
L237: Changed in version 3.8: Falls back to 【81†`__index__()`】 if 【135†`__complex__()`】 and 【136†`__float__()`】 are not defined.
L238: Deprecated since version 3.14: Passing a complex number as the real or imag argument is now deprecated; it should only be passed as a single positional argument.

L240: delattr(object, name, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【17†¶】
L241: This is a relative of 【61†`setattr()`】. The arguments are an object and a string. The string must be the name of one of the object’s attributes. The function deletes the named attribute, provided the object allows it. For example, `delattr(x, 'foobar')` is equivalent to `del x.foobar`. name need not be a Python identifier (see `setattr()`).

L250: dir()【19†¶】
L251: dir(object, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))
L252: 
L253: 
L254: Without arguments, return the list of names in the current local scope. With an argument, attempt to return a list of valid attributes for that object.
L255: If the object has a method named 【145†`__dir__()`】, this method will be called and must return the list of attributes. This allows objects that implement a custom 【146†`__getattr__()`】 or 【147†`__getattribute__()`】 function to customize the way `dir()` reports their attributes.
L256: If the object does not provide 【145†`__dir__()`】, the function tries its best to gather information from the object’s 【148†`__dict__`】 attribute, if defined, and from its type object. The resulting list is not necessarily complete and may be inaccurate when the object has a custom 【146†`__getattr__()`】.
L257: 
L258: The default `dir()` mechanism behaves differently with different types of objects, as it attempts to produce the most relevant, rather than complete, information:
L259:   * If the object is a module object, the list contains the names of the module’s attributes.
L260: 
L261:   * If the object is a type or class object, the list contains the names of its attributes, and recursively of the attributes of its bases.
L262: 
L263:   * Otherwise, the list contains the object’s attributes’ names, the names of its class’s attributes, and recursively of the attributes of its class’s base classes.
L264: The resulting list is sorted alphabetically. For example:
L265: 
L266:     >>> import struct
L267:     >>> dir()   # show the names in the module namespace
L268:     ['__builtins__', '__name__', 'struct']
L269:     >>> dir(struct)   # show the names in the struct module
L270:     ['Struct', '__all__', '__builtins__', '__doc__', '__file__',
L271:      '__initializing__', '__loader__', '__name__', '__package__',
L272:      '_clearcache', 'calcsize', 'error', 'pack', 'pack_into',
L273:      'unpack', 'unpack_from']
L274:     >>> class Shape:
L275:     ...     def __dir__(self):
L276:     ...         return ['area', 'perimeter', 'location']
L277:     ...
L278:     >>> s = Shape()
L279:     >>> dir(s)
L280:     ['area', 'location', 'perimeter']
L281: Note
L282: 
L283: Because `dir()` is supplied primarily as a convenience for use at an interactive prompt, it tries to supply an interesting set of names more than it tries to supply a rigorously or consistently defined set of names, and its detailed behavior may change across releases. For example, metaclass attributes are not in the result list when the argument is a class.
L284: 
L285: divmod(a, b, / (Positional-only parameter separator (PEP 570)))【20†¶】
L286: Take two (non-complex) numbers as arguments and return a pair of numbers consisting of their quotient and remainder when using integer division. With mixed operand types, the rules for binary arithmetic operators apply. For integers, the result is the same as `(a // b, a % b)`. For floating-point numbers the result is `(q, a % b)`, where q is usually `math.floor(a / b)` but may be 1 less than that.
L287: In any case `q * b + a % b` is very close to a, if `a % b` is non-zero it has the same sign as b, and `0 <= abs(a % b) < abs(b)`.
L288: enumerate(iterable, start=0)【21†¶】
L289: Return an enumerate object. iterable must be a sequence, an 【149†iterator】, or some other object which supports iteration.
